title: Fungal Structures and Reproduction
question: How do fungal structures help with feeding, dispersal and making new cells?

blocks.prompt: Required before observations: Is the mushroom above a log the whole fungus? Predict what might also be inside the log.
blocks.text: The mushroom may be the visible reproductive part, with fungal threads inside the wood.

blocks.prompt: Required before observations: A spore lands on a surface. Predict what it needs to start growing, and why landing would not immediately make a mushroom.
blocks.text: A spore may need water and usable nutrients, then growth and compatible mating before a mushroom forms.
Timing: Before lens, spore or budding observations.

Inspect one supplied mushroom-forming fungus and one budding yeast example. They illustrate different structures and processes, not repeated trials. Compare the mushroom with its mycelium, then follow one spore and one budding event. No live culture or real rate measurement is involved.

The mycelium is a feeding network; the mushroom is a spore-producing fruiting body.
Correct after feedback.
Lens views are supplied illustrations, not student measurements or independent organisms.
One model basidiospore released into an air gap.
Moist wood
Landing conditions accepted for this example. Surface choice revised after feedback.
Model growth phases viewed: 2/2. The model supplies the growth response; the student chooses and interprets it.

A thin thread grows from the spore and branches into a young mycelium.
Correct first check.
The basidiospores belong to a sexual life cycle; only release, germination and early growth are shown. Compatible mating and later fruiting requirements are omitted.
Model phases viewed: 3/3. Student marked the attached bud before later division/separation.

A smaller daughter grows as a bud and separates after the nucleus divides.
Correct after feedback.
Nuclear information is a supplied explanatory overlay; this asexual event does not represent every yeast life cycle.
Distinguish feeding hyphae and mycelium from a mushroom fruiting body.

blocks.prompt: Use the two lens views to compare mycelium and mushroom gills. Which part spreads through the wood, and which part supports spore production? Revisit your first prediction.
blocks.text: My body explanation: the threads form feeding mycelium, while mushroom gills carry spore-producing basidia. One spore on supplied moist wood grew a hypha and branches, not an instant mushroom; compatible mating and later growth still matter. The yeast daughter grew from an attached bud and received genetic material before separating. That budding was asexual, while the supplied basidiospores belong to a sexual cycle. These model views are not independent cultures or measured growth rates.

blocks.prompt: How does this fungus obtain nutrients from the wood?
blocks.text:
Enzymes break material down outside the hyphae; the cells absorb usable molecules.
Correct! Fungal enzymes break down nearby material. Hyphae absorb the resulting small molecules. The mushroom and mycelium are parts of the same fungus. Correct on first recorded check.

blocks.prompt: Do spores always show asexual reproduction?
blocks.text:
No. Fungi can make spores through sexual or asexual life cycles.
Correct! Spore means a reproductive cell, not one universal process. The basidiospores in this mushroom example belong to a sexual cycle involving meiosis. Other fungi also make asexual spores. Revised after feedback.

blocks.prompt: What is supported by the yeast sequence shown here?
blocks.text:
One parent makes a daughter by budding and mitosis; no mating is shown.
Correct! This is asexual budding. DNA is copied and mitosis provides genetic material to mother and daughter. Mutations can occur. The sequence does not show every yeast life cycle. Correct on first recorded check.

All specimens, colors, enlargements and growth changes are original teaching illustrations, not recordings or measured cultures. The surface choices use stated model conditions, not a controlled test of every factor. The example fungus can use the supplied wood; other species need different conditions. The basidium shown has four spores; the number varies among fungi. Only one spore is tracked. Its release into an air gap and later transport are shortened; the water-drop launch mechanism is omitted. Germination does not complete the sexual life cycle or guarantee a mushroom. Compatible mating and suitable conditions are omitted later requirements for this mushroom example. Yeast nuclear details are explanatory overlays; DNA copying and mitosis have additional steps. Growth is untimed. The shown budding is asexual, but yeasts can also have sexual cycles. No species, edibility or clinical identification is established, and no physical culture instructions are provided.
